court: New York Common Pleas, Special Term
holding_summary: The court held that the plaintiff's building, though it might fall within general definitions of a hotel, was not chargeable as a 'hotel' under the municipal water-rate ordinance given its actual (deficient) water supply and use as a cheap lodging house. The extensive per-room hotel tax therefore did not apply, and the matter instead fell under the ordinance's residual special-contract provision. The court granted an injunction restraining the Croton Aqueduct Board from cutting off the water supply for non-payment of the disputed tax.

I shall, therefore, grant the injunction.

The ordinance of the city corporation, establishing the rate of water rents, provides that hotels and boarding houses shall, in addition to the regular rate for private families, be charged for each lodging room, at the discretion of the Croton Aqueduct Board.

notes: Primarily a municipal water-tax classification dispute (hotel vs. lodging house), not a licensing/regulation case in the police-power sense; polarity marked mixed because it neither restricts nor affirmatively protects the letting practice but extensively addresses its legal characterization.

holding_summary: The court held that the Act of 1860, which gives boarding-house keepers the same lien as innkeepers upon the goods of their boarders, applies even where board is furnished under a special contract at a fixed weekly or monthly rate, not merely in circumstances analogous to a transient innkeeper's guest. Because the plaintiff owed the defendant three weeks' unpaid board, the defendant's lien on his trunk was valid, and the district court's contrary judgment for the plaintiff was reversed.

quotes.text: The act of 1860 for the protection of boarding-house keepers (L. 1860, c. 446),—giving to boarding-house keepers the same lien for board upon the goods of boarders which an innkeeper has upon the goods of a guest, . —applies to cases of special contracts for board at a fixed rate by the week or month, although an innkeeper would, under such circumstances, have no lien.
Misch boarded with O’Hara, who was a boarding-house keeper, and owed her for three weeks’ board, when she demanded his room, and requested him to leave her house.

It has been held in the cases cited by Judge Yah Hoeseh, that the intent of the statute was to give a boarding-house keeper the lien which an innkeeper has upon the effects of his guest, without reference to the question whether the guest was a transient one or a boarder by the week or month, at a rate agreed upon or fixed.

holding_summary: The court held that a defendant who merely let rooms to lodgers, without supplying meals, and who had leased the building's basement restaurant to an independent operator, was not an innkeeper, since an inn furnishes both food and lodging under one management. Because mere lodging-house keepers have no lien on a lodger's effects either at common law or under New York's statutes (which extend a lien only to boarding-house keepers), the defendant's claimed lien on the plaintiff's property failed, and the judgment below was affirmed.

quotes.text: The conclusion of the judge that the defendant was not an innkeeper was correct. He merely kept a lodging house, in which no provision was made by him for supplying the lodgers with meals, and such house is not an inn (Cromwell v. Stephens, 2 Daly 15), as an inn furnishes both food and lodgings to the guests.
It is plain, therefore, from these cases, that one who merely lets out rooms to lodgers had, at the common law, no lien upon the effects which the lodger had in the room.
so that the question must be regarded as remaining the same as it was at common law, that mere lodging house keepers have no lien upon the effects of the lodger.

holding_summary: The court held that the statutory lien given to boarding-house keepers under the 1860 Act attaches only to board actually due at the time of detention and cannot be extended to cover future or contingent board obligations. Because the boarder's account had been paid in full before she left, no debt existed to support a lien, so the trial court properly directed a verdict returning the property to the plaintiff.

quotes.text: The statute providing for the protection of boarding-house keepers, {Laws of 1860, p. 771,) gives a lien upon the effects of boarders for the amount which may be dm for board, and it cannot be extended to any other indebtedness, nor to any demand not due at the time of the detention. It does not include board to become due under an agreement to board in future.

The act which provides for the protection of boarding house keepers, (Laws of 1860, p. 771,) gives the lien upon the effects of the boarders for the amount which may be due for board, and it cannot be extended to any other indebtedness, nor to any demand not due at the time of the detention.
There was not, therefore, a present indebtedness; which was essential to give a boarding house keeper’s lien upon the property of his guest.

holding_summary: The court held that renting a hotel room at a fixed weekly price does not by itself convert a guest into a mere boarder or lodger; because the plaintiff had not bargained for any particular length of stay and was shown to be a wayfarer, the relation of innkeeper and guest existed between the parties. As such, the innkeeper was subject to the common-law rule of strict liability for unexplained losses of a guest's property absent contributory negligence, and the judgment for the defendant was reversed.

quotes.text: We are of opinion that the relationship of innkeeper and guest existed between the parties.

The common law holds the innkeeper absolutely liable for all thefts from within, or unexplained losses of property in his charge, belonging, to his guest, although he may be discharged from liability by any contributory negligence of the guest.

But a special agreement fixing in advance the price to be paid, or the length of the stay, does not absolutely disturb the relation of innkeeper and guest, and constitute the person so acting a boarder or lodger.

notes: Facts state a $1.25/week room rate but do not establish how long the plaintiff had actually occupied the room; duration marked unclear rather than 'weeks' since that figure is the price basis, not the occupancy length at issue.

court: New York Common Pleas, General Term
holding_summary: The court held that a boarding-house keeper is liable for the loss of a boarder's goods caused by the negligence of the keeper's own servants acting within the scope of their employment, applying the general master-servant liability rule to boarding-house keepers. A boarding-house keeper must exercise the same due and reasonable care over a boarder's property that a prudent person would take of his own, and on the facts presented (a stranger negligently admitted alone to the plaintiff's room) the defendant was liable, though the damage award was reduced for lack of proof of value on some articles.

quotes.text: It is incumbent on a boarding-house keeper to exercise due and proper care of the baggage or property of his boarder— such care as a prudent person would take of his own property.
A boarding-house keeper is liable for the loss of his guest’s goods, occasioned through the negligence of his own servants while they are acting within the scope of their employment.
I know of no good reason why a boarding-house keeper should be an exception to this rule.

holding_summary: The court held that the 1860 Act protecting boarding-house keepers confers upon them no greater lien rights than innkeepers possessed at common law, and that a lien attaches only to the effects of the person actually liable for the unpaid board. Because the plaintiff's husband alone had contracted for and become liable for the couple's board, the wife incurred no personal liability, and the defendant therefore had no right to detain the wife's separate wearing apparel for the husband's debt; the judgment for the plaintiff was affirmed.

quotes.text: Held, that chapter 446, Laws of 1860, for the protection of boarding-house keepers, confers upon them no greater rights than inn-keepers possessed at common law.

court: City Court of New York, General Term
holding_summary: Following McIlvaine v. Hilton, the court held that a boarding-house keeper has no statutory lien on the separate personal effects and wearing apparel of a boarder's wife where the husband alone contracted for and became liable for board furnished to himself and his wife. Because the wife incurred no liability for the board debt, her goods could not be detained to satisfy her husband's obligation, and the judgment for the plaintiff-wife was affirmed; the court also held it was within its discretion to allow amendment of the pleadings and excuse a procedural default.

quotes.text: A boarding-house keeper has no lien on the separate personal effects 'and wearing apparel of the wife living at the boarding house with her husband, where the husband was received under a contract to furnish board for himself and wife.

court: Supreme Court, General Term, First Department
holding_summary: A householder who let two rooms in her occupied dwelling to a lodger for a fixed 8.5-month term, with board included, created a lease and landlord-tenant relationship rather than a mere board-and-lodging agreement. The lodger's estate remained liable for rent for the full term, subject to an offset for the cost of board saved after her death, and the landlord was entitled to interest on each weekly installment from when it fell due.
